title: Foundations
description: How an LLM call works, how models use tools, the agent loop, and how to defend it against prompt injection.
outcome: Explain, message by message, what happens when software talks to a large language model. Describe a tool to a model and keep your code in control of what actually runs. Recognise an agent loop, set limits on it, and name the main defences against prompt injection.
audience: Anyone starting with AI agents: developers adding their first AI feature, product managers who need to reason about cost and risk, students, and security analysts who will review AI systems. No machine-learning background is needed.
build: Three small, runnable programs in Python and TypeScript: a stream reader that refuses to treat a cut-off answer as finished, a safe tool-calling loop with validation and round limits, and the agent-loop and injection-defence labs inside this path. All run offline with a scripted model, so you need no API key.
prerequisites: Comfort reading short snippets of JSON helps. Programming is optional for the lessons and needed only for the labs.
body:
Every AI product you will meet, from a chat window to an autonomous security agent, is built from the same few moves. An application sends a request to a model. The model replies one token at a time. Sometimes, instead of answering, it asks your code to run a tool. Repeat that cycle and you have an agent. This path walks through those moves in order, and each lesson builds on the one before.

Start with **What happens when you prompt an LLM**. You will see why a chat app re-sends the whole conversation on every turn, why tokens rather than words drive cost and speed, and how to tell a finished answer from one that hit the length limit. These details sound small, but they explain most surprising bills and most "the AI stopped mid-sentence" bug reports.

**Tool use** shows how a model asks for a weather lookup, a database query or a ticket to be created, without ever running anything itself. The key idea is the boundary: the model proposes, your code decides. You will learn where validation, permissions and secrets belong, and how results flow back with matching IDs.

**The agent loop** turns that single round trip into a cycle that keeps going until a goal is met. You will see why agents need budgets for steps, tokens and time, and how to stop one that is going in circles.

The path ends with **Prompt injection and guardrails**, because the moment an agent reads web pages, emails or documents, someone else can try to give it instructions. You will learn why instructions alone are not a defence, and how least privilege, approval gates and logging limit the damage when a model is fooled.

The whole path is free. Each lesson has an interactive simulation with Beginner, Practitioner and Expert explanations, a step-by-step guide, a quiz and sources you can check.

title: Knowledge & Protocols
description: Give agents knowledge and connections: RAG, memory, context engineering, and the MCP and A2A protocols.
outcome: Design how an agent gets the right information into its context: retrieval for documents, memory for what it learned earlier, and caching for what it reuses. Connect agents to tools with the Model Context Protocol, secure remote MCP servers with OAuth, and decide when agents should talk to each other through A2A instead.
audience: Developers and architects building assistants over company knowledge, platform teams exposing internal tools to AI, and security reviewers assessing how agents connect to systems.
build: Labs in Python and TypeScript, including retrieval and memory exercises, an in-process MCP-style JSON-RPC server and client, and protocol exercises for remote MCP and A2A, each with tests you can run offline.
prerequisites: The Foundations path, especially Tool use and The agent loop.
body:
A model only knows what is in its context window for the current request. This path is about getting the right information there, and nothing else, at a sensible cost.

**RAG** (retrieval-augmented generation) searches your documents first and pastes the best passages into the prompt, so answers can cite your handbook instead of guessing. You will see how chunking, embeddings and search quality decide whether the answer is right. **Memory** covers what an agent should remember across sessions, how to summarise long conversations, and when to forget. **Context engineering and prompt caching** shows how to order and trim what you send, and how providers reuse a stable prompt prefix to cut cost and latency.

The second half turns to connections. The **Model Context Protocol** gives any AI application one standard way to discover and call tools, resources and prompts from a server. **Remote MCP** follows the same protocol over the network, with the Streamable HTTP transport and OAuth-based authorization, and the security mistakes to avoid when an agent acts on a user's behalf. Finally, **A2A** (Agent2Agent) covers how independent agents find each other, hand off tasks and return results, and how that differs from MCP, which connects an agent to tools rather than to other agents.

Every protocol lesson uses real method and field names from the specifications, with the revision and the date they were last checked.

title: Building Reliable Agents
description: Reasoning and structured outputs, workflows vs agents, multi-agent teams, computer use, human approval, evals, observability and cost.
outcome: Choose between a fixed workflow and an autonomous agent for a task, get dependable structured output from reasoning models, and keep agents safe and affordable in production with human approval, evaluations, tracing and budgets.
audience: Engineers and technical leads taking agents from demo to production, and the product and risk owners who sign off on them.
build: Labs including an approval gate, an evaluation harness, structured-output validation with retries, a minimal tracer for agent runs, and a cost calculator that enforces a per-task budget.
prerequisites: The Foundations path. Knowledge & Protocols is helpful but not required.
body:
Demos are easy; reliable agents are not. This path covers the decisions and safeguards that separate the two.

It opens with **Reasoning models and structured outputs**: how models that think before answering trade tokens for quality, how to control that effort, and how to make output machine-readable with JSON Schema so the next step in your system can trust it. **AI workflow automation** then draws the line between a fixed pipeline with one smart step and a fully autonomous agent, and why the simpler option is often the right one.

**Multi-agent teams** and **Computer use** cover two ways agents grow: splitting a large job across specialist agents with their own context, and operating software through the screen when there is no API. Both are powerful and both are expensive or fragile if used carelessly.

The last four lessons are about running agents responsibly. **Human-in-the-loop approvals** put people in charge of risky actions without slowing everything down. **Evals** turn real tasks into repeatable tests so a prompt or model change cannot silently make things worse. **Observability** traces every model call, tool call and retrieval so you can debug a bad answer. **Cost and latency budgeting** shows how to predict and cap spend and response time, and how to measure cost per completed task rather than per request.

title: AI for Security Teams
description: Automate security operations with software agents and AI agents, safely: triage, phishing, playbooks, hunting, response, vulnerabilities, cloud and access.
outcome: Design AI-assisted security operations where endpoint agents observe and act, AI agents investigate and propose, and analysts approve anything disruptive. Apply the pattern to alert triage, phishing, SOAR playbooks, threat hunting, incident response, vulnerability remediation, cloud misconfigurations and access reviews.
audience: SOC analysts, detection and response engineers, security architects and IT leaders evaluating AI for security operations, and developers building security automation.
build: A reference triage agent with risk-tagged tools, argument validation, approval gates, hourly action limits and an audit log, plus security labs for specific workflows, all in Python and TypeScript with tests. The Build guide works as the capstone project.
prerequisites: The Foundations path, especially Tool use and Prompt injection. Basic familiarity with security operations concepts such as alerts, SIEM and EDR helps.
body:
Security teams face more alerts than people can read, and attackers move quickly once inside. AI agents can investigate around the clock, but only if they are wired up carefully: with good data, narrow permissions and people in charge of disruptive decisions.

The path starts with **Software agents + AI agents working together**, which sets the pattern used throughout: small programs on every machine collect evidence and carry out approved actions, while an AI agent decides what to check and what to propose. From there, each lesson applies the pattern to a real workload.

**AI alert triage** and **Automated phishing analysis** handle the highest-volume work in most security operations centres. **SOAR playbooks** show which steps can safely run automatically and which need approval. **Threat hunting** turns a hunch into log queries and then into a permanent detection. **Incident response** keeps a timeline and follows the playbook while people make the calls. **Vulnerability fixing**, **cloud misconfiguration fixes** and **access reviews** cover the slower, preventive work where AI saves days rather than minutes.

Every lesson uses documentation-reserved IP addresses and example domains, maps behaviour to MITRE ATT&CK where relevant, and cites standards such as NIST guidance. The capstone **Build guide** explains how to put the pieces together in your own environment, with a tested reference implementation.
